replies.text:
A major newer study is Anahit Hovhannisyan et al., “Demographic history and genetic variation of the Armenian population,” American Journal of Human Genetics, published November 2024 / January 2025 issue. It used whole-genome data from Armenians whose grandparents came from different regions of the Armenian Highland and compared them with ancient genomes from the region. The researchers found that modern western, central, and eastern Armenians are relatively homogeneous and that modern Armenians partly overlap genetically with ancient inhabitants of the eastern Armenian Highland, supporting regional continuity going back thousands of years. 

One of the clearest studies is Ashot Margaryan et al., “Eight Millennia of Matrilineal Genetic Continuity in the South Caucasus,” Current Biology (2017). Researchers analyzed complete mitochondrial genomes from 52 ancient individuals from present-day Armenia and Artsakh spanning about 7,800 years, then compared them with 206 modern Armenian mitochondrial genomes and neighboring populations. Their key result was that the lowest genetic distance was between modern Armenians and the ancient individuals from the region, and their demographic modeling strongly favored continuity of the maternal gene pool over major population replacement.

There was also a 2020 study by Movsesian and colleagues titled “The Bronze and Iron Age populations of the Armenian Highland in the genetic history of Armenians.” This one studied 498 ancient and modern crania using nonmetric skeletal traits, rather than sequencing complete genomes. It found close biological relationships among Late Bronze Age, Early Iron Age, and modern Armenian groups and concluded that the evidence reflected deep continuity in the formation of the Armenian population, with relatively limited major changes since the Late Bronze Age.

replies.author: @ImArkando
replies.text:
The DNA of Armenian people today is not "almost identical" of the DNA of those historical peoples (especially Hayasa, since it's more nuanced/plausible with Urartu) because there is no possible way to guarantee a genetic relationship to that extent. Through dating and inspection of ancient skeletons, DNA can be found that unites a group of people into one, and records from outside can tell a story of their culture and some continuity can be established with the people of the modern Armenian highlands, but... while these may be, to a limited extent, similar to existing ethnic groups (such as Armenians or Georgians), there is no way to determine any exact or "identical" relationship between them. The Urartu also spoke a different language, from a completely different language family.


It is even more difficult to determine any relationship with Hayasa-Azzi - those were ancient peoples documented pretty much only from the outside. Certain scholars believe their existence played a role in the ethnogenesis of Armenians (which is probably what you're referring to), but there is no evidence and no way to gather evidence that would directly link their genetics or language to modern Armenians.

The video also doesn't state things from any "ultra-Armenian" point of view, that's a narrative you installed.

I'm not commenting this because I'm against Armenians or anything like that, but seeing people present assertions of historical evidence, I felt like it had to be corrected. It's wrong to lay out a genetic continuity of "Hayasa → Urartu → Armenian kingdom → modern Armenians". That's far too linear for what the actual evidence allows scholars to say.

comments.text:
My friend, I watched your videos, especially the one about your trip to Azerbaijan.

I understand that you have many Armenian friends, and that the information they share with you has influenced the way you have formed your understanding of the relationship between these two countries.

However, I believe there are several important omissions in the part of your video about Karabakh. If it would be useful for you and your viewers, I would like to briefly mention a few missing details.

You said that the modern borders were drawn during the Soviet period in 1921. However, just three years earlier, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Armenia had declared their independence and established their own borders. These were the modern borders of the region. When the Russians arrived, they redrew and changed these borders in a biased way.

Another important point is that the Karabakh conflict entered its second phase in 2020. The first phase began in 1991, when Azerbaijan had just regained its independence. As Soviet military forces withdrew from the region, they took much of the weaponry in Azerbaijan with them. At the same time, Soviet weapons and even Russian military units remained present in newly independent Armenia.

Encouraged by this military advantage, Armenian forces occupied Karabakh and seven surrounding regions. Those facing them were not a regular army, but mostly civilians. During this period, one of the bloodiest episodes in modern Caucasian history took place — namely, ethnic cleansing, to put it bluntly. More than one million Azerbaijani civilians were displaced and became refugees. This situation continued until 2020.

What happened in 2020 was the return of more than a million displaced civilians to their homes.

I would also like to mention that while thousands of Azerbaijani civilians were killed during the military operations in 1992, not a single Armenian civilian was killed during the military operations in 2020. Instead, Azerbaijani cities located many kilometers away from the war zone were targeted by rocket attacks, and Azerbaijani civilians were killed once again.

Perhaps these additions will not be welcomed by your Armenian friends, but these are factual realities. If we truly want peace, everyone must acknowledge what they did.
